newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen opening up but bevy of data looms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen opening up but bevy of data looms.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected open higher Thursday, unless a major surprise emerges from the heavy slate of economic data due before the open.
Analysts said stocks would draw on the momentum from their late recovery yesterday, a rebound that cut nearly half the sharp losses posted in the first half of a jittery session.

"We had kind of an irrationally exuberant sell-off yesterday," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "You have to watch what happened when we closed and when we closed we were recovering."
Analysts said investors yesterday showed some of the same resilience they mustered last Friday, when comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan spooked the market.

"For the second time in a week, the market showed its ability to bounce off a low," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "That shows there's still buying out there when the market dips far enough."
Even so, they cautioned, the fact that stocks are able to survive the dips did not necessarily mean a new leg of the rally was about to begin.
"We still have the same problem -- nosebleed," Wachtel said. "Blue chips are at lofty levels and need a little rest and rehab up here."
At 0830 EST/1330 GMT, markets will receive a slew of information, including the Consumer Price Index and retail sales for November, as well as weekly jobless claims.

Economists forecast a 0.3 percent rise in the CPI and a 0.2 percent increase in the core rate, which excludes food and energy. Retail sales are expected to rise 0.3 percent, 0.2 percent excluding automobile sales. New jobless claims are seen rising to 341,000 from 336,000.
In Tokyo, stocks ended slightly lower, with the Nikkei-225 closing at 20,501, down 67 points for the session.
U.S. shares were firm in London and the FTSE-100 rose 18 points to edge fractionally over the 4000 level.
The dollar was mixed Tokyo, falling slightly against the yen but up against the mark. In Europe, the dollar firmed past the 113 yen and 1.54 mark levels.
U.S. Treasuries worked their way back from yesterday's sell-off, with the 30-year bond up 17/32 to yield 6.59 percent.
The December S&P 500 index future rose two to 741.55.
The New York Times Marketplace column reports that mutual fund inflows were strong in November but new money to stock funds seems to have tailed off in early part of December.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column focuses on the recent rally in Intel Corp, which is picking up steam as executives meet with Wall Street professionals to discuss the company's outlook.
